title: Why Students Like Playing Sports More Than Learning Math
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer explains why many kids prefer sports to math by naming three features of the sports learning environment: it admits endless expressions of thought, it returns rich information on each attempt, and it lets you try again right away. He contrasts this with much math software, which offers a handful of permissible answers and returns only right or wrong. Dressing that low-information feedback in growth-mindset messages or confetti does not make it useful. He extends the critique from software to curriculum and classrooms and proposes two evaluative questions: how many students get to express how many kinds of thinking, and how many then get something interesting to think about in response. The conclusion is that teaching is the work of attaching meaning to student thinking. The closing links are incidental.
points: Sports feel good to learn because a nearly unlimited range of attempts is possible and each one produces meaningful feedback.
Right or wrong feedback from math software is low information and does not tell learners what part of their thinking worked or what to try next.
Cosmetic additions like growth mindset messages and confetti cannot rescue weak feedback design.
Meyer's two audit questions can be applied to software, curriculum or a lesson.
Teaching is defined as attaching meaning to as many kinds of student thinking as possible.
quotes: Many kids like playing sports more than they like learning math, and I’m starting to understand why.

Whatever shot you take—literally any shot—the world around you immediately returns volumes and volumes of useful information. Whether or not the ball goes in is one of the most important and interesting pieces of information, sure, but there are others before and beyond that one.
There are infinite ways to shoot a basketball, infinite ways to shoot it successfully, and even unsuccessful shots are interesting.
The fact that you can try your shot again, often from the same exact spot, adds enormous incentive to learn from your missed shots. You can put your new learning to immediate use.
In a lot of math software, you’re allowed four possible thoughts. If none of them reflects your thoughts, you’re unlikely to feel the same agency someone feels when they play a sport.
It doesn’t matter if we dress the “wrong” feedback up with a growth mindset message or the “right” feedback up with computer confetti. It isn’t useful feedback. It’s low information.
That’s it. The work of teaching is to attach meaning to as many kinds of student thinking as possible. That seems harder in some disciplines than in others and I can’t stop wondering why.
